name: Docker, Inc. (formerly dotCloud)
origin_detail: Founded as dotCloud in 2008 in Paris by Kamel Founadi, Solomon Hykes and Sebastien Pahl; incorporated in the US in 2010; renamed Docker, Inc. on 2013-10-29. HQ Palo Alto, California.
openness_notes: The engine's open-source upstream, Moby, is Apache-2.0, and Docker contributes to CNCF projects such as containerd and runc. Docker Desktop is proprietary: since 2021-08-31 larger businesses (250+ employees or $10M+ revenue) need a paid subscription. Revenue comes from Desktop/Hub subscriptions on top of an open engine: level 2. The 2013 open-sourcing date and original licence were not stated in fetched pages.

license_history.note: Moby described as the open-source components Docker and the community built for the Docker Project.

license_history.license: Docker Desktop: paid Pro/Team/Business subscription for larger businesses
license_history.note: Free for fewer than 250 employees AND less than $10M revenue; grace period to 2022-01-31; from $5 to $21 per user per month (2021 prices, since revised).

relicensing_events.from: Docker Desktop free for all users
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Followed by a $105M Series C (March 2022) citing more than 4x year-on-year ARR growth and 56,000 paying customers.

exit_events.note: Mirantis bought the Docker Enterprise platform business, its team and 'hundreds of enterprise customers' on 2019-11-13; terms confidential. Docker, Inc. restructured with a $35M recapitalisation.

risk_events: 2019-11: Enterprise business sold to Mirantis; restructuring and $35M recapitalisation
2021-08-31: Docker Desktop subscription requirement for larger businesses
2025-02: CEO change (Don Johnson succeeded Scott Johnston)
robustness: The runtime pieces live in Moby (Apache-2.0) and CNCF projects (containerd, runc), so containers do not depend on Docker, Inc. The company depends on proprietary Desktop and Hub subscriptions: 56,000 paying customers and 16M monthly active users in March 2022. It acquired MCP Defender (AI-agent security) in September 2025 (Wikipedia citing Docker blog).
openness_effect_assessment: Open-sourcing Docker made the company a unicorn by April 2015, but it could not monetize the runtime and sold its enterprise unit in 2019. It recovered by charging larger companies for the proprietary Desktop app from 2021, which coincided with more than 4x ARR growth: the money came from closing developer tooling, not the open core.
key_takeaway: Docker is the case of an open project that won its market so completely that the company struggled to capture the value: Kubernetes and the clouds monetized containers, Docker sold its enterprise unit in 2019, and then rebuilt around paid Desktop subscriptions for large companies. Value capture came from a proprietary client, not from relicensing the engine.
